newsitem.title: USA: Clinton 'fundraising plan' stirs fresh controversy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton 'fundraising plan' stirs fresh controversy.

text.p: A top Democratic National Committee fundraiser and a White House official conceived a plan to raise millions of dollars from Asian-Americans for this year's campaign by offering rewards, including access to President Bill Clinton, the New York Times reported on Saturday.

The newspaper said the plan -- arguably unseemly but on its face apparently not illegal -- was among 3,000 pages of DNC documents on the cascading Clinton campaign fundraising controvery made public in recent days.

It said Democratic fundraiser John Huang and Doris Matsui, a deputy assistant to Clinton for public liaison and wife of Representative Robert Matsui, a California Democrat, devised the plan to meet the party's goal of raising $7 million from Asian-American donors.
The report brought a sharp rebuttal from the White House, which said the Times had "erroneously confused" two different groups.
"Mrs Matsui has indicated that she was not involved in the development of any fundraising strategy described in the story," White House special counsel Lannie Davis said.

"She did not engage in any fundraising for the Democratic National Committee or the Clinton campaign, and did not ever read or was ever consulted about the campaign plan referred to by the New York Times."
He added that Clinton had "complete confidence" in Matsui and was grateful for her public liaison work.

Davis said that Matsui directed an Asian Pacific American Working Group that had as its aim "community outreach and increasing involvement of Asian-Pacific Americans" in U.S. political and civic life.

He said the Times had apparently mixed up this group with a fundraising entity called the Asian Pacific American Leadership Council. It was not immediately clear if the two groups had a common membership or were otherwise linked.

A substantial portion of the money raised from Asian-American donors has since been found to have been collected from questionable or improper sources, embarrassing the president and his fellow Democrats and triggering several ongoing probes.

The New York Times said the fundraising plan specified that people who donated at least $10,000 and companies that gave $15,000 or more were to be rewarded "by inviting them to special White House or other events" with the president.
Previous Republican administrations used similiar tactics to court big campaign contributors, although they were usually not as blatant about it.
The newspaper said the meetings often included discussion of Clinton's policies toward Asian nations, though no evidence has surfaced that contributors influenced those policies.
